```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 120 else 60
)
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444", "#b23b3b")
```

Every run starts from a state: water in the soil store, in each routing store, and in transit
through the outlet delay. A poor starting state produces a spurious flood or a spurious
drought until the model forgets it. For a 29-year calibration that matters little, because a
warm-up period absorbs it. For a short test run or a forecast it can dominate the result.

pdmS7 offers four kinds of start.

| Start | Function | What it assumes |
|---|---|---|
| Cold | `initial_state(model, soil_fraction = 0.5)` | Soil at a fixed fraction of capacity; routing stores empty |
| Warm, from an observed flow | `initial_state_from_flow(model, observed_m3s, baseflow_fraction)` | The catchment is in steady state with the flow at the start |
| Warm, by spin-up | `spin_up(model, forcing, cycles)` | Repeating a forcing period settles the stores |
| Hot | The final state of a previous run | Nothing: the model simply continues |

The same starts are available from other languages through the core: `pdm_initial_state()`,
`pdm_state_from_flow()`, and passing the state array from one run to the next.

# An experiment

The reference below is a catchment simulated continuously for a year. At the end of that year
we start a 60-day run from each kind of start and compare it with the reference. The first
week is dry, as it often is at the start of a test period.

```{r experiment}
set.seed(3)
model <- pdm_model(area_km2 = 50)
make_forcing <- function(n) {
  data.frame(rain = ifelse(stats::runif(n) < 0.06, stats::rgamma(n, 0.7, scale = 3), 0),
             pet = 0.08)
}
history <- make_forcing(24 * 365)
period <- make_forcing(24 * 60)
period$rain[1:(24 * 6)] <- 0

year <- run_pdm(model, history, initial_state(model, 0.5))
true_state <- year$state
observed_start <- year$output$q_end_m3s[nrow(history)]
reference <- run_pdm(model, period, true_state)$output$q_m3s
round(observed_start, 3)
```

The steady-state start needs the share of the flow that is baseflow. In practice you would
estimate it, for example from the National River Flow Archive's baseflow index for a UK
gauged catchment. Here we show two guesses: a good one (0.9) and a poor one (0.5).

```{r starts, fig.cap="Left: the first 30 days of each run against the reference (thick grey). Right: each run's error on a log scale; values below 0.0001 m3/s are drawn at the bottom of the axis."}
starts <- list(
  "Cold, 50% soil" = initial_state(model, 0.5),
  "Cold, 90% soil" = initial_state(model, 0.9),
  "Warm, from flow (share 0.9)" = initial_state_from_flow(model, observed_start, 0.9),
  "Warm, from flow (share 0.5)" = initial_state_from_flow(model, observed_start, 0.5),
  "Warm, spin-up" = spin_up(model, period, cycles = 3),
  "Hot, previous state" = true_state
)
runs <- lapply(starts, function(s) run_pdm(model, period, s)$output$q_m3s)
days <- seq_along(reference) / 24
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 2, 1), cex.main = 0.95)
plot(days, reference, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "grey70", xlim = c(0, 30),
     ylim = c(0, max(unlist(runs), reference) * 1.05), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)",
     main = "First 30 days")
for (i in seq_along(runs)) lines(days, runs[[i]], col = pal[i], lwd = 1.5, lty = i)
legend("topright", c("Reference", names(runs)), col = c("grey70", pal),
       lty = c(1, seq_along(runs)), lwd = c(3, rep(1.5, length(runs))), bty = "n", cex = 0.65)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(1e-4, 30), log = "y", xlab = "Day", yaxt = "n",
     ylab = "Error (m3/s, log scale)", main = "How long each start takes to forget")
axis(2, at = 10^(-4:1), labels = c("0.0001", "0.001", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10"), las = 1,
     cex.axis = 0.8)
for (i in seq_along(runs)) {
  lines(days, pmax(abs(runs[[i]] - reference), 1e-4), col = pal[i], lwd = 1.5, lty = i)
}
```

```{r errors}
first_week <- seq_len(24 * 7)
data.frame(
  start = names(runs),
  mean_error_first_week_m3s = round(vapply(runs, function(q) {
    mean(abs(q[first_week] - reference[first_week]))
  }, numeric(1)), 4),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

# What the experiment shows

- **A cold start manufactures a flood.** With empty routing stores and a half-full or nearly
  full soil store, the soil drains rapidly into groundwater and the model produces a peak many
  times the true flow, in dry weather. The 90 per cent start is worse than the 50 per cent
  start: guessing "wet" is not safer.
- **The steady-state start removes most of that error.** It starts from the observed flow,
  and the remaining error comes from the assumption that the catchment is in equilibrium. Even the poor baseflow guess beats a cold start by more than an order of
  magnitude.
- **Spin-up does about as well as a good steady-state start** here, but it needs forcing to
  repeat and it settles towards the forcing period's own average conditions, not the
  conditions on the start date.
- **A hot start is exact**, as it should be: restarts are exactly continuous.

In this catchment every start converges within about three weeks. A catchment with a slower
groundwater store remembers its start for longer, sometimes for months, which is when the
choice matters most.

# Recommendations

- **Calibration over many years:** any start, followed by a warm-up period of at least a few
  months that is simulated but not scored (the `warmup` argument of `calibrate_pdm()`).
- **Short test runs:** a steady-state start from the first observed flow, preferably at the
  start of a dry recession, when the steady-state assumption is closest to the truth.
- **Operational forecasts:** a hot start from the previous run, then `correct_state()` at the
  forecast origin. See [Forecast updating](forecast-updating.html).
- **Restarts:** keep the final state of each run. It is a complete record of the model's
  memory, and continuing from it reproduces an unbroken run exactly.
